P1-T011.notes: The authority rule is docs/architecture/CONFIG_AUTHORITY.md's sentence as code: a layer cannot widen what a layer above it allows, and cannot weaken a restriction a layer above it imposed. New file crates/sure-core/src/config/authority.rs. Layer is User and Project and nothing else -- rank 3 (organization policy) is not a variant, so no caller can name a source it can never obtain, and rank 1 (the person at the keyboard) is not configuration and stays in ConsentGrantor::InteractiveUser. Layer::can_grant is a match, not 'self == Self::User', so a third layer must answer the question. Authority::privileges() records every ask including refused ones -- request, every layer that asked (most trusted first), grantor or None -- because dropping refusals would make 'asked and refused' and 'never asked' the same list. A grant comes only from the topmost layer that asked and only if that layer may grant; a project and its user both asking is not an escalation. permissions() is not decide(): it says which permissions a file was allowed to hand over, and the execution mode is deliberately not a permission, so a project asking for host_confirmed gets nothing in the set. Restrictions resolve the other way -- protection and privacy take the stricter of the two layers with Resolved::by naming the most trusted layer that asked -- and 'by: None' means 'nothing beyond the default' rather than 'SURE did not look'. Ranks are hand-written matches rather than a derived Ord, with the two unavailable variants ranked in the safe direction. No merged Config (ADR 0011); scope reductions are reported, never overridden. P2-T002.notes: crates/sure-core/src/fingerprint/ (digest.rs, git/mod.rs, git/status.rs, error.rs, mod.rs) + tests/fingerprint_git.rs (34 tests on Windows, 37 on Unix) + docs/architecture/FINGERPRINTING.md; scan/ignore.rs gained left_out() so the fingerprint and the scan cannot disagree about which directories are out of scope. Acceptance criterion 1, HEAD/dirty tracked diff/relevant untracked state affect fingerprint: the digest is over the project's file contents, not over Git's diff, because a diff changes when the same files are committed, amended or rebased while the project state a check would read has not. HEAD is digested and the branch name is not -- the branch is recorded in GitState for a person to read, and two branches at the same commit are the same state. A deletion and an empty file are two states (the Gone arm writes a marker, not the digest of empty content). A clean project has no change digest at all, rather than the digest of an empty list, so clean and empty-list are two states and not one; the domain type says so with an Option and the code follows it. Acceptance criterion 2, fingerprint changes on relevant source changes: every change record contributes the file's own path and its contents, and the untracked tree is walked file by file. Digest framing: the domain tag sure.git-fingerprint.v1 is the first field, every field is written length-then-bytes so (ab,c) cannot hash equal to (a,bc), and an absent optional field writes a presence byte rather than an empty string. SHA-256, because the project being fingerprinted is written by a coding agent and an adversary choosing a collision is in scope, not hypothetical. Git is asked for status with --untracked-files=all --no-renames -- . plus a separate rev-parse --show-prefix. --relative is deliberately absent and is now forbidden by a comment and by a mutation: on this machine's Git 2.55.0.windows.3 it prints nothing at all for a repository with changes and exits 0, which is an empty change list indistinguishable from a clean tree -- a dirty project would have fingerprinted clean and every check keyed to it would have gone green. It was caught by a_dirty_project_fingerprints_differently_from_a_clean_one, not by reading the flag list. The prefix is stripped with Path::strip_prefix, not string comparison, so a project in app/ is not confused by a sibling app-old/. A nested checkout that Git reports as one untracked directory is walked and read; a walk that loses something is FingerprintError::IncompleteTree, never a hash of a partial tree; the byte budget is over the whole fingerprint and a file that crosses it is an error, never a prefix hash. ProjectFingerprint::matches compares kind and digest and never id. Three of them found real holes in an already-green suite and the tests that close them were written afterwards: (1) Reader::tree -- the whole nested-checkout walk, its per-file path digest and its IncompleteTree guard -- was reached by no test at all; (2) the monorepo test proved only stability, so an implementation that never stripped the prefix, looked every path up at root/prefix/..., found Gone and hashed nothing passed every assertion it made; (3) the byte budget had only ever been exercised with one file, which cannot tell a per-file budget from a per-fingerprint one. The script reports BUILD for a mutation that fails to compile rather than counting it as caught, and SKIP for an anchor that does not match exactly once, after the first version of two mutations were a no-op and a compile failure respectively. NOT VERIFIED ON THIS MACHINE: the three #[cfg(unix)] tests (two link tests and the unreadable-file test) have never run here -- Windows cannot create a symlink without Developer Mode or administrator rights, both probed and absent, and the WSL here has Git 2.53.0 but no cargo. One of the three was rewritten this session without having run anywhere. Their verification is the ubuntu-latest and macos-latest CI jobs, which RUST_DESIGN.md names as the designed path for Unix-only behaviour; the Windows job passing says nothing about them. No dispatcher between Git and content fingerprinting is provided: choosing is P2-T003's decision, and fingerprint/mod.rs says so. HARDENED AFTER ACCEPTANCE: a security review of 9f13f0d found the fingerprint could still be made to run a program the repository chose, and it was right -- the fix was incomplete. A tracked .gitattributes names a filter driver and the repository's own configuration gives it a command, so a plain git status executes it; measured with a marker program and a positive control, and it fires with nothing modified. It cannot be switched off: there is no Git flag that disables in-tree .gitattributes (git help --config lists only the global core.attributesFile), the driver name is not known until Git has read the project so there is no fixed -c to pass, and overriding it anyway would be worse than refusing -- with the filter off Git compares raw bytes against a blob written through the filter and calls every such file modified, a wrong fingerprint rather than an absent one. So the repository is refused, with the new FingerprintError::RepositoryRunsPrograms naming the settings it found. The check is one extra invocation, git -c core.fsmonitor=false --no-pager config --list --includes -z with GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=<root>/.git/config/sure-no-global-configuration, run AFTER rev-parse (measured not to run a filter) and BEFORE status (measured to run one -- a check that came after would be a report). That path cannot exist on any platform because .git/config is a file in every repository Git makes, including linked worktrees and submodules, so no project can add settings to the answer about itself. --local is not used and the reason is measured: it does not follow include.path without --includes and misses .git/config.worktree even with it. CORRECTION MADE IN THIS COMMIT: --includes was documented as load-bearing and it is not -- git config --list with no scope named already follows includes, measured after a mutation showed dropping the flag failed only the pinning test and no behavioural test. The flag is kept, the claim is corrected in the source, in FINGERPRINTING.md and in the test. BOUNDARY, MEASURED AND LEFT OPEN: a repository can still reach a filter defined by the MACHINE's config by naming the driver in .gitattributes (target/tmp/boundary_probe.sh, and both C:/Program Files/Git/etc/gitconfig and ~/.gitconfig carry filter.lfs.* here). It is left open because the project cannot choose the program, only ask for one the user installed, which is not project-controlled executable code -- the line EXECUTION_SAFETY.md draws. Documented in FINGERPRINTING.md and raised in HANDOFF.md rather than folded into this fix. 34 mutations in target/tmp/mutate6.py, 34 fired, 8 of them new for this check; the two most valuable are 'the check runs after the status instead of before it', which is caught only by the assertion that the marker does NOT exist, and 'the suppressed global path is one a project could create'.

P2-T003.notes: crates/sure-core/src/fingerprint/content.rs (the manifest), choose.rs (which kind a project gets), read.rs (the path-reading machinery both kinds share: Reader, Contents, file_kind, display_path) + tests/fingerprint_content.rs (23 tests) + tests/fingerprint_git.rs unchanged at 43 + docs/architecture/FINGERPRINTING.md (a content-fingerprint section, the dispatch rule, gaps 8). Acceptance criterion 1, scoped content manifest is deterministic: the manifest is a SHA-256 over the walk's files and links, sorted by the text that goes into the digest rather than by the paths, with the path digested beside the contents so that a move or a name swap is a change. Two copies of one project in two directories agree (two_copies_of_one_project_are_one_fingerprint), which is what proves no absolute path reaches the digest. Every limit -- max_depth, max_entries, max_files, max_bytes -- is an error and never a digest over the part that fitted. Acceptance criterion 2, generated/vendor churn is excluded by documented rules: the walk IS crate::scan, the same tables and the same comparison the checks use, so the exclusion is not a second list that can drift. the_excluded_list_is_the_scans_and_not_a_second_copy_of_it pins the agreement rather than the list; churn_in_every_excluded_kind_of_directory_changes_nothing rewrites one directory per SkipReason (build output, vendored, caches, .venv, .sure) and asserts the digest does not move, with the control that a covered file does move it -- without that control a fingerprint that never moved at all would pass. a_repositorys_own_storage_is_out_so_a_commit_does_not_move_the_manifest makes an empty commit, asserts the ref really moved, and then asserts the manifest did not. The decision this task owned, and it is the reason choose.rs exists rather than a boolean in a caller: a project is fingerprinted by Git when it is at the ROOT of the working tree containing it, not merely inside one. rev-parse --show-prefix is empty exactly then. A directory one level inside somebody else's checkout gets Content, because the Git kind would digest the OUTER repository's HEAD -- a commit anywhere else in that repository moves the subdirectory's fingerprint although not one of its files changed, and evidence marked stale for a project nobody touched is how a person learns to ignore the word. That is measured, both ways, in the_git_kind_moves_for_a_commit_the_project_is_not_part_of_and_the_content_kind_does_not, which also asserts the Git kind still DOES move, so the reason cannot quietly become folklore. A machine without Git is GitUnavailable and NOT a fallback to Content: the kind has to be a function of the project and not of the machine, or one unchanged directory is two fingerprints on two machines and never agrees with itself. A FALSE GREEN THIS TASK FOUND IN ITS OWN TESTS. The first version of the test named a_project_in_no_repository_at_all_is_fingerprinted_by_content used a fixture under target/, which is inside the SURE checkout and therefore inside a working tree -- so it was exercising the 'somebody else's repository' branch and never the 'no repository' one, and it passed. Nothing about the assertion was false and nothing said the fixture could not reach its case. The mutation 'a directory in no repository is refused rather than read by content' was MISSED by every test, which is what surfaced it. Fixed by Fixture::outside_any_repository (the system temp directory) plus git_prefix(), which asserts the premise with git directly -- a premise checked with the code under test is not a premise. The same premise assertion was added to the 'inside somebody else's repository' test. Held by reasoning rather than by a test, and recorded as gap 8 rather than left to look covered: the sort before hashing, and the domain tag. target/tmp/mutate7.py applies 16 mutations, all caught, and reports the two link mutations BLIND on Windows. Removing the sort passes every test, because one run sees one filesystem's order and a digest is a value -- there is nothing for a test to compare two of; setting the tag to the Git kind's also passes every behavioural test, because the two digests cannot collide even with one tag (Git opens with 'head', content with 'manifest'), so the tag is belt and braces over the field structure and is pinned by a constant assertion instead. Two mutations that were MISSED until the script was made to run --test fingerprint_git too: read.rs is shared, and the walk inside a nested directory is only ever reached through the Git kind. The file limit and the byte budget tests were also both boundary-weak and were strengthened: max_files now asserts both sides of three files under limits of three and two, and the byte budget is now shown to be spent by the whole manifest rather than by each file. One earlier claim was corrected rather than quietly dropped: the two-kinds-cannot-collide test comment said it was 'belt and braces over the domain tags', which the mutation showed is not what makes the two digests differ.

Acceptance -- detects Cargo workspaces/packages and conventional commands -- is met by: A Cargo.toml IS A DOCUMENT WITH TWO SIBLING TABLES, `[package]` and `[workspace]`, AND EITHER CAN BE ABSENT. That single fact is what the module is arranged around. A manifest with only `[workspace]` is a virtual manifest, and it declares a great deal -- the members, their shared dependencies, their shared lint levels -- so the workspace tables are held on `Manifest` and NOT on `PackageSection`, and `Manifest` is a separate type for that reason. The first draft hung them off the package, where a virtual manifest's entire workspace, the case such a manifest exists for, would have been dropped; mutation 24 reverts exactly that decision and is caught. A third fact is kept apart from both and is not a convenience: `[dependencies]` is meaningful only where `[package]` exists, because Cargo refuses a virtual manifest that declares dependencies. The same split decides the commands, and this is the second designed-out bug rather than a discovered one: `command_for` gates on `project.manifest.manifest()?` -- the DOCUMENT -- and deliberately not on `package()`. Gating on the package would have withheld every command from a workspace root, which is a project `cargo build` acts on and builds every member of. The comment at that line says so, mutation 23 deletes the gate and is caught, and a test covers the virtual-manifest case directly. Members are resolved by the same `pattern` module Node uses -- one `*` per path segment, lifted into discover/pattern.rs so the two ecosystems cannot come to expand a glob two ways -- and the resolution reports what it could NOT resolve as data rather than dropping it. AN `exclude` LIST IS NOT SUBTRACTED: whether a directory named by both `members` and `exclude` is a member is Cargo's rule and SURE has not read it, so `Workspaces::excluded_members` carries the overlap and neither list is applied. Reporting the overlap is reversible by a reader who knows the rule; silently honouring it would be SURE asserting a rule it cannot cite. Mutation 19 makes `exclude` delete the member and is caught. THE TOOLCHAIN PIN IS READ BY THE FILE'S NAME, because the two names say different amounts: `rust-toolchain.toml` holds a `[toolchain]` table (channel, components, targets, profile) and the bare `rust-toolchain` is not TOML and usually holds one token. `toolchain_from_text` therefore branches on the name and not on what parsed -- a `.toml` that parses but carries no `[toolchain]` table is WrongShape, a `.toml` that does not parse is NotParsed, and only a file that is not TOML falls through to the bare-channel reading. This is the one place a filename changes an answer and the doc says so. Components are matched without regard to case, and `ToolchainState::asks_for("clippy")` answers false for Absent as well as for Unread, so the one question a caller may collapse is the one that collapses to false. Tooling comes from a 22-crate table over four ToolRoles, with the finding naming the table's own crate spelling and never the project's. A SECOND COMMIT COMPLETED THIS TASK RATHER THAN EXTENDING IT, and it exists because the first commit's own tests were wrong twice. A background security review flagged crates/sure-core/src/discover/pattern.rs, the module this task had just lifted out of node.rs. Reading it independently found the containment rule sound -- no traversal, no filesystem reach, no unbounded expansion -- and found the real gap underneath: THE MODULE HAD NO TESTS AT ALL, 209 lines of behaviour that decides which directories SURE reads, reachable through three callers and therefore checked three ways and stated nowhere. Nine tests were added against a real walk (`scan` and `Tree::of`, the same pair production uses, so a walk that changed shape fails here rather than being papered over by a hand-built tree), and a fourth family of mutations (28-34) was anchored on pattern.rs so those tests are shown to be load-bearing rather than counted as coverage: a pattern that climbs out refused in every position, including the two that begin with a directory that genuinely resolves; an absolute pattern refused where the PLATFORM says it is absolute, so `C:\Windows` is refused on Windows and is one ordinary file name on Unix; an unexpandable pattern refused rather than partly expanded; the root named by `.` and never a member of itself; `*` naming directories and never files; two patterns reaching one directory naming it once; a refusal told apart from a pattern that named nothing; the platform's case rule rather than a spelling; and every reason a pattern can fail for being nameable and describable. THE FIRST VERSION OF THOSE TESTS TURNED THE SUITE RED, AND THE MUTATION RUN IS WHAT SAID SO: the scratch helper used the process id, and `discovery_runs_none_of_the_scripts_it_reads` greps the TEXT of all six files in the module tree for the process module's name, `#[cfg(test)]` code included. The suite was therefore failing before any mutation was applied and every CAUGHT in that run was unattributable -- and this is exactly the fault a person checking their own work would miss, because `cargo test --lib discover::pattern` is green either way. The fix is in the test and not in the check, because the check was right about the file: uniqueness now comes from `create_dir` failing rather than from a name, which is strictly stronger, because a process id is unique within one run and says NOTHING across two -- a name built from it collides with a previous run's directory when the OS hands out the same id, and the test then reads a fixture some earlier run had already written into, where `create_dir` refuses to adopt a directory that exists. It then went red a SECOND time, on the sentence explaining the fix: the sentinel searches raw text, so a doc comment reading "no `std::process` here, deliberately" tripped the very check it was describing. A mention is not an ability, and the test now drops whole-line comments before searching -- only whole-line ones, so every line that can hold code is still searched. Neither fault was visible in a diff; both were found by running something that was expected to pass. Both are now rules the harness enforces instead of steps a person remembers: the suite is run UNMUTATED first and a red baseline ends the run with BASELINE IS NOT GREEN, and the compiler-error list is kept separate from the FAILED list so that an error line reaching stdout cannot return CAUGHT for a suite that did not compile. The doc gained six enforced-by rows for the new tests, one rewritten row recording that the no-process check reads source text and drops comments, and a gap 16: an `exclude` pattern that is refused, or that names nothing, leaves no trace. That does NOT misstate membership -- `excluded_members` means "these resolved members are also named by exclude", and an empty list is true in every one of those cases -- but it costs a reader the ability to tell an `exclude` list SURE could not follow from one that named nothing, and the two are worth telling apart because a member list cut off by `max_workspace_members` computes its overlap against the truncated list. The enforced-by index was re-checked mechanically rather than by eye: 88 backticked identifiers, of which 87 are `#[test]` functions and one is a deliberately named function (`read_manifest`), and 0 are found nowhere. P2-T009.notes:
P2-T009 — implement README/spec command and claim extraction.

Acceptance: "Extracted commands are untrusted documentation and never
auto-executed merely because documented."

DELIVERED. `sure_core::documents` (crates/sure-core/src/documents.rs): a
`DocumentReport::of(&Discovery)` that finds the project's documents, reads each
one's fenced code blocks, and returns a `DocumentedCommand` per command line —
carrying the text as one string, the shell family the fence named, whether a
prompt marker was removed, the heading it sits under, the document and the
1-based line. Plus crates/sure-core/tests/document_commands.rs (20 tests).

The acceptance's first half is a label: every command reaches the intent model
as `IntentSource::ProjectSpec`, *derived* from `Config::goal_source()` rather
than restated, so a project file is documentation here for the same reason it is
documentation in `support::classify`, and there is still one place that decides
it. A `DocumentedCommand` is the claim and there is one list rather than two: a
fenced block carrying a language is the only claim a document makes that SURE
can read off by rule, and pulling requirements out of a sentence would be the
T17 hallucination. `lying-readme`'s description ("README setup command does not
work on fixture") and `P4-T005`'s acceptance both read it that way.

The second half is about something that did not happen, which is the kind of
claim that is easy to write and hard to hold. It is held by asserting three
things together — the command was found, the document was read, and a recursive
snapshot of the project is byte-identical before and after — with a control
proving the snapshot helper can see a new file, because a helper that never
notices anything would satisfy the first assertion perfectly. The fixture's
command is `npm install && echo SURE-RAN-THIS > SURE-RAN-THIS.txt`, so the
evidence of a leak is a file whose absence is checkable rather than an inference.

"Never auto-executed" is a property of the shape rather than a promise. No field
on `DocumentedCommand` can hold a program and its arguments, no shell-splitting
exists anywhere in `sure-core`'s shipped code, `DocumentReport::of` is the only
door a report can come through, and `sure-cli` builds no `DocumentReport` at
all. The module declines the stronger claim in as many words: there is no
function that turns a `DocumentedCommand` into an `ApprovedCommand`, so the path
does not exist rather than being blocked.

Indentation is ignored when looking for a fence, and that is the one deliberate
departure from CommonMark: a fence inside a list item is indented by the marker
width, so following the spec exactly reports no commands *and* a complete
reading, which is a silent loss dressed as a clean result.

P2-T011.notes:
P2-T011 — implement intent source tracking (provenance/trust labels).

Acceptance: "Intent sources preserve provenance/trust labels." and "Inferred
intent cannot satisfy user requirements."

DELIVERED. `sure_core::intent_model` (crates/sure-core/src/intent_model.rs, 14
unit tests) and crates/sure-core/tests/intent_sources.rs (7 tests), plus
`pub mod intent_model;` in lib.rs and a corrected PROJECT_INTENT.md.

The acceptance's first sentence is a claim about a label *surviving*, and a test
can hold it wrongly by reading the label off and agreeing with it. So every test
that asserts a label here also drives the statement through
`may_claim_full_fulfilment`, which is the gate the label is actually for. The
second sentence is held by driving an intent of nothing but guesses through the
same gate and asserting it cannot reach zero requirements short.

THE SHAPE, which is the whole design. Every channel has a **door**: a function
that produces a `Requirement` and writes its own `IntentSource`. No function here
that produces a `Requirement` takes an `IntentSource` as an argument, so a caller
holding a command it read out of a README has nothing to ask for — there is no
parameter to ask with. Provenance survives by a shape the module does not offer
an alternative to, rather than by a rule its code follows. The one function that
does take a source, `from_source`, goes the other way: it reads statements *back*
by the label they arrived with, and the module comment names it rather than
leaving a reader to find it and doubt the rule.

`observed_user_request` takes an `&Authority` and not a `&Config`, and the same
bytes on disk give opposite answers. `sure.yaml` lives inside the project, and
the project is written by the same agent whose work is being judged, so
`privacy.full_recording: true` there is a **request**;
`Authority::privilege(ProjectRequest::FullRecording)` is asked whether anyone was
able to grant it, and only the user's own settings outside the project can. The
integration test holds one `sure.yaml`, byte for byte, refused first as an
escalation and then granted — with a control asserting the kept request is worth
exactly what a goal that was typed is worth, because the privacy decision is
about whether the words are kept and not about how much they count.

Six rows in the module's table and five labels: `documented_goal` and
`DocumentReport::as_requirements` are one channel reached by two doors, and both
ask `Config::goal_source()` rather than naming the label themselves, so P2-T009's
decision point is still the only one. `documented_goal` answers `None` for a goal
with no words rather than manufacturing a blank requirement, and it keeps the
project's own spacing — the test feeds it a padded goal, because a door that
tidied the words and still set `raw_retained` would be reporting something it did
not do. `agent_claim` and `inferred` leave `raw_retained` false: the claim door
does not know whether the caller kept the agent's sentence or restated it, and an
inference has no original wording behind it at all.

A test of my own made a claim it could not hold and was deleted rather than
reworded. `a_documented_goal_is_labelled_by_the_one_place_that_decides_it`
compared the door's answer against `Config::goal_source()` and its comment said
"this is the assertion that fails on that day" — but no test can move a `const`,
so the mutation that writes the literal is invisible to that comparison and the
test would have passed for a different reason than its name said. The claim is
now declared unobservable in the harness with the condition that would falsify
it, and a distinctness test replaced it. Three claims in the module's own comment
were likewise false and were found by reading it against the code before the
harness ran: it said "no function takes an `IntentSource`" (`from_source` does),
"one of the four channels" (`IntentSource::ALL` has five), and that `P8-T005`
*writes* an observed request, present tense about a `queued` task.

THE SHAPE. One `ProcessRequest` carries every item of the acceptance's first
sentence as a required field — program, arguments, working directory, environment
and cancellation, with the deadline and both output bounds together in `Limits` —
so a caller cannot start a program without having decided each one. The
environment is an enum, `Environment::Only` or
`Environment::Inherited { without, with }`, rather than a map whose default is to
inherit, because "pass on everything SURE has" and "pass on these three variables"
are different intentions and a default silently picks one of them. `Outcome`
answers what became of the run with a `Termination` that keeps the cases apart
rather than smoothing them: `Exited { code }`, where `code` is `None` for a
process the operating system ended with a signal rather than a fabricated number,
`TimedOut` and `Cancelled`, each carrying a `Stop` saying whether the whole tree
was reached, and `CancelledBeforeStart` — a separate answer from `Cancelled`
because a caller that cancels a `cargo test` and one that cancels a `service
start` care about opposite things. It carries the start time, the duration, each
stream's kept bytes and each stream's discarded byte count.

THE SECOND SENTENCE IS THE BUILDER, AND IT IS ONE PLACE.
`request.rs:398` is the only `command()` in shipped code: `Command::new(&self.program)`,
then `command.args(&self.arguments)` — one element per argument, no joining, no
quoting — then `command.current_dir(&self.working_directory)`. There is no string
anywhere in this path that gets split, and the module documentation says so at the
place a reader would go looking for the shell. What it does **not** claim is that
a batch file cannot run, because that would be false and the module says so: a
name with no extension is completed to `.exe` and nothing else, so a bare `npm`
is not found even where `npm.cmd` is on `PATH`, but a `.cmd` or `.bat` named
*with its extension* does start and the process that runs is `cmd.exe`, which
Windows supplies. A `.ps1` does not start at all. All three are measured, and
`tests/process_runner.rs` holds each as a test. `terminate.rs` reaches the whole
tree with `taskkill /T /F` rather than by signalling one process, because
`CLAUDE.md` makes process-tree cancellation on Windows a first-class requirement.

`tests/spawn_sites.rs` HOLDS "NOTHING RUNS YET" AS A TEST RATHER THAN A SENTENCE.
One test asserts every place SURE builds a `Command` is named in that file; the
other asserts that nothing outside the runner names a process request at all. So
"no product path runs a program yet" fails the day it stops being true, instead
of going quietly stale in a document. `fingerprint_git.rs` was extended in the
same pass, and **it is worth saying that it failed first**: it forbids the
stored-program spelling `Command::new(&self.program)` outside

another name, and the new runner tripped it. That was the check working — it
found a second stored-program `Command` in shipped code and made somebody decide
whether it was a second way to start Git. It is not: the runner holds any program
a caller names and has no mention of Git in it. So it is exempted **by name**,
rather than by loosening the rule, and `Command::new("git")` stays forbidden
everywhere including inside the runner, so a Git invocation could not hide in it.

A PATH IS FIVE DIFFERENT THINGS IN ONE REQUEST, AND THE THIRD SENTENCE NAMED ONE.
The working directory was covered, in the one position the operating system takes
as a value of its own. A path is also the **program**, which has to survive being
turned into a command line by somebody; an **argument**; a value in the
**environment block**, a second encoding surface with its own conversion; and, in
reverse, the **bytes coming back out** of a program. Four tests now hold the four
that were missing, over one `const AWKWARD` ("a directory with a space and
é中文") and one `const NOT_ASCII` ("héllo wörld 中文 🎉"), so that "a path with a
space and a character outside ASCII" means one thing everywhere it is used.
`NOT_ASCII` carries three different problems rather than one, because the three
fail differently: `é` is what a byte-oriented path passes through and a code-page
conversion does not, `中文` is what only a real encoding survives, and `🎉` is
outside the Basic Multilingual Plane — two UTF-16 code units, one surrogate pair
— which is the case a conversion that stops at the first unit truncates.

THE TREE TEST'S CENTRAL ASSERTION PROVED NOTHING ON WINDOWS, AND THAT WAS
MEASURED RATHER THAN ARGUED. Its claim is "a stop reaches the whole tree" and its
evidence was that the grandchild's report never appeared — but **a file that is
absent is what a stopped grandchild leaves behind and also what a grandchild that
never ran leaves behind**. Measured twice on this machine: with the grandchild's
mode string changed to a name that is not a test, and the new marker assertion in
place, the test fails saying the grandchild never started; with that assertion
removed — the old reading — the same run passes, in 3.26s, reporting `WholeTree`
about a tree that never existed. On Unix the same change fails loudly, because
that branch asserts the opposite outcome, so the hole was in the branch that
skipped a measurement.

The fix is a positive control. `child_waits_to_be_released` writes
`<report>.started` the moment it is running and then waits for `<report>.release`;
the parent asserts the marker **before** it reads the absence, so "the stop
reached it" and "it never existed" can no longer be confused, and afterwards it
drops the release to ask the second question by the only means both platforms
have — a process that is running writes within a poll and a process that was
stopped cannot write at all. Waiting on a file instead of sleeping also takes the
clock out of the test: the old grandchild slept 1.5s, which must be long enough
not to finish before the stop and short enough to be worth waiting out, and on a
fast machine the first of those is what breaks.
`a_cancelled_run_reaches_what_it_started_too` holds the same claim for the
caller's decision rather than the runner's clock, cancelling only after the marker
exists so the test cannot race two process starts.

THE FOUR MATRIX TESTS ARE CHARACTERISATION TESTS, AND SAYING OTHERWISE WOULD BE A
FALSE CLAIM. No mutation of the runner as it stands can make them fail:
`OsString` round-trips on Windows, and a `to_string_lossy` step applied to valid
Unicode is the identity, so every way of breaking them first has to introduce a
conversion the code has never had. What they are for is the rewrite that reaches
for one — a raw command line, a job object, a hand-built environment block — and
they are recorded as characterisation rather than dressed up as
mutation-covered. The one mutation added to `mutate18.py` this time is about the
position that can be got wrong in the code as written: *"the program path is
quoted, in case it has a space in it"*, the plausible mistake, since a path with a
space is the reason to quote and the process API quotes the program itself. It is
caught, and measured directly, by the new test among others — with it applied,
`a_program_at_a_path_with_a_space_and_unicode_is_the_program_that_runs` fails
alone in 0.01s with `os error 123`, `ERROR_INVALID_NAME`, before any process is
started.

ordinary missing name in the same directory produces. A control rather than a
literal, because the sentence the operating system supplies is localized (this
machine answers in Chinese) and only the `(os error N)` suffix is stable.

neighbouring case and **checks nothing SURE wrote** — it asserts a premise about

P3-T004.notes:
P3-T004 — command classification.

Acceptance: "Static/read-only, dynamic host, install, network, destructive
categories are distinct."

DELIVERED. `crates/sure-core/src/safety.rs` is new and is the first thing in the
product that reads a command line at all: `classify()` takes a program name and an
argument vector, not a `ProcessRequest`, and answers with a `CommandEffects` — the
set of categories the command *may* fall into — plus a `Source` saying why. The
five categories live in the domain beside the permissions they already answer
with: `CommandClass`, one wire name each, and `CommandEffects` as a canonical set
with `union`, `contains`, `is_static_only` and a `ungrantable()` door. One commit,
`967c5e6`, five files: `crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs` +414,
`crates/sure-core/src/safety.rs` +1278, `crates/sure-core/tests/command_safety.rs`
+637, `crates/sure-domain/tests/wire_contract.rs` +10/-1, and one line in
`crates/sure-core/src/lib.rs`. **Purely additive**: 424 insertions and 1 deletion
across the tracked files, and the deletion is an import line that got longer.

THE ACCEPTANCE SENTENCE IS SATISFIED BY CONSTRUCTION AND BY TEST, AND THE TWO ARE
NOT THE SAME CLAIM. Distinctness by construction is the enum and its frozen wire
names; distinctness as a fact about behaviour is a test that takes **every ordered
pair of the five** and shows a command can be told apart under one from under the
other, over a witness table with one single-category command per category. The
witnesses are `git status`, `npm test`, `cargo add serde --offline`, `git fetch`
and `git reset --hard`, and the test asserts the witness table is as long as
`CommandClass::ALL` — so a sixth category with no witness fails the test rather
than passing quietly. `rustc` cannot tell a category apart from a category, and
that is the gap those tests close.

**THE ONE RULE THE MODULE IS ARRANGED AROUND: nothing is `Static` unless a rule in
the file says so.** A program with no row, a known program with an operation the
table has no name for, and a command line whose meaning is in text SURE cannot
read all come back as *every category but `Static`*. That is the only mistake here
that nothing downstream could catch, and it is held by a test named for the
sentence — `nothing_sure_could_not_read_is_ever_static` — which walks the unknown
programs, the unknown operations and the four wrappers. A fourth cause is handled
the same way and is easy to miss: an argument that is not text SURE can read makes
the whole line unread rather than being dropped, because dropping one token from
`git <bytes> status` would leave SURE reading the `status` behind the bytes and
answering `Static` about a command line it did not read.

**`Destructive` HAS NO PERMISSION THAT COVERS IT, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.**
`required_permission()` answers `None` for it. `WriteProject` is writing *inside*
the project, which `rm -rf ..\..\` is not, and `git push --force` is not a write at
all; folding it in would let a consent to write a file read as a consent to
destroy the machine. `ungrantable()` is the door a caller uses to find that out,
and a test holds it. What *should* cover it is `P3-T005`'s question, and answering
it here would have put a permission decision inside the classifier.

**ONE CORRECTION DURING THE WORK, AGAINST MY OWN FIRST TABLE.** `python -m pip
install` was filed as `Install` alone and an integration test caught it: the
domain's `ActionKind::InstallDependencies` has `executes_project_code()` true and
`can_touch_network()` true, because a source distribution is built by a build
backend the package brought with it and npm runs lifecycle scripts. The domain was
the authority; the table was wrong. Everything that may run a package's own
install steps is `INSTALLS_AND_RUNS`; `RESOLVES` is what cargo's manifest-only
operations get. That integration test walks the command set SURE's own discovery
builds — `cargo test`, `npm test`, `npm run build`, `python -m pytest`,
`python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`, `uv sync`, `poetry run pytest` — so a
change that stops classifying one of them fails rather than going unnoticed.

**THE VOCABULARY GAP IS STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER.** The acceptance names
five categories and none of them is "changes files in this directory without
destroying anything". `git commit` and `git branch -m` are therefore
`UnknownOperation` — not `Static`, and not a sixth class invented here, which
would have made the acceptance sentence untrue by satisfying it. `git pull` *is*
classified, because one of its effects is one the vocabulary has. `git branch`,
`tag`, `config`, `remote`, `stash`, `cargo clean` and `npm audit` are absent on
the rule the module writes down: a verb is in the table only when every form SURE
can name has an effect SURE can name.

A NAME IS READ THE WAY THE OPERATING SYSTEM RESOLVES IT, and the condition is
`cfg!(windows)` rather than `#[cfg(windows)]` — both arms compile and the
difference is a value. That is `P3-T003`'s lesson applied rather than restated, and
this run is where it was checked: the test that holds the rule is present and runs
**on all three platforms**, reading each platform's own arm, rather than being
deleted on two of them. A `.cmd` or `.bat` name reads as unread text whatever it
is called and whatever is in it, because a name is not evidence of behaviour —
and a caller that wants to name one is a finding for the owner, recorded below
rather than dodged.

P3-T005 — the execution permission and consent plan.

Acceptance: "Check plan can explain which commands need permission and why." /
"Denied command becomes skipped/not checked, never pass."

DELIVERED. One commit, `c940300`, six files. `crates/sure-core/src/consent.rs` is
new at **1407 lines** and is the file that joins the three things this product has
been building separately: `P3-T004`'s classifier, the decision, and the check
plan. Two additions in the domain carry facts the plan needs and must not restate
— `CommandClass::plain_description` (`execution.rs` +54, of which the method is
24 lines and its test 30) and `CheckPlan::exclude` (`vocabulary.rs` +67, of which
the method is 27 lines and its two tests 40) — one line adds the module to
`lib.rs`, and `tests/spawn_sites.rs` is +65/−1, most of which is a false positive
I fixed in the check rather than by renaming a type.

THE SECOND ACCEPTANCE SENTENCE IS STRUCTURAL, NOT TESTED-INTO-EXISTENCE.
`PlannedCommand::refusal` is the only place this module produces a `CheckResult`
and it cannot produce a passing one: a command that may run returns `None` —
because what to report about it depends on what happens when it does, and nothing
has happened yet — and a refused one returns `CheckResult::not_run`, which is
`Skipped` with its reason *and its weight* kept. The weight is what stops a
skipped `MustFix` critical check from aggregating away, and the test walks eight
cases asserting the status, the reason, the weight and `!aggregate(&[result])
.is_green()`, with a vacuity guard that at least six of the eight are actually
refusals. A mutation that reported a `Pass` there, and a second that kept the
reason but zeroed the weight, are both caught.

THE THREE RULES, IN `decide`'s ORDER, AND THE ORDER IS THE RULE.

1. **A missing permission denies.** Every category the command may fall into is
   checked; one permission the user has not granted is enough. First because it is
   the only one of the three that is not a question.
2. **A category with no permission is never covered by a grant.**
   `CommandClass::Destructive` answers `None` to `required_permission()` — left
   that way deliberately by `P3-T004`, which named this task as the one that had
   to answer for it — so there is nothing to grant and the command needs its own
   approval. `ADR 0009`'s rule for arbitrary commands, applied to the other thing
   SURE cannot bound. Checked *before* the mode because a cautious mode is a
   question to ask and a missing permission is not.
3. **The mode, last.** A command that runs project code under a mode that runs
   nothing comes back `NeedsConsent` rather than `Denied`: a mode that is too
   cautious is a question with an answer.

`Destructive` STILL HAS NO PERMISSION, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER TO `P3-T004`'s
RECORDED QUESTION RATHER THAN A DODGE OF IT. The question was where the "writes
inside the project" category lives. It does not live anywhere yet: a command that
merely *writes* is still outside this vocabulary, exactly as `P3-T004` found, and
this task did not invent a sixth category to close it — the acceptance names five.
What this task answers is the other half: a category the user cannot grant is not
a gap in the permission set, it is a command that needs its own approval naming
its exact argument vector, and `awaiting_own_approval`, `ungrantable` and the
explanation's "No permission SURE can ask for covers this" line are that answer.

THE FINDING, AND IT WAS IN MY OWN FIRST VERSION OF RULE 3. `runs_project_code`
over a set of categories is `DynamicHost` **and `Install`**: installing a package
runs that package's own install steps and builds source distributions with the
backend it shipped. The first draft tested only `DynamicHost`, so `npm install`
under `inspect_only` came back `Denied` where
`decide(ActionKind::InstallDependencies, …)` answers `NeedsConsent` — a check
reported as impossible that was merely unasked. **The test that found it runs both
deciders over every category that has an `ActionKind`, in every mode and under
both a read-only and a fully granted permission set, and requires them to agree.**
It is the reason the second decider could be written out at all: it is written out
rather than delegating because a set can hold categories no single `ActionKind`
describes, and the agreement test is what makes that safer than a second opinion
rather than more dangerous.

**ONE CORRECTION TO MYSELF, FOUND WHILE WRITING THE CONSENT TEST FOR IT.**
`CheckPlan::exclude`'s first version recorded the reason unconditionally while its
own doc comment said a check the plan never held is *not* recorded at all — the
code and the paragraph disagreed, and the paragraph was right. `excluded` now
means exactly "checks this plan contained and then took out", and the caller's
`false` is the whole of what the method can say about a check that was never
there. `PermissionPlan::exclude_refused_from` returns those ids to the caller
rather than absorbing them, because a command planned against a check the plan
does not contain means two check sets were assembled into one plan. **This is a
correction inside the task's own uncommitted work rather than to anything that
shipped**, and it is recorded because the two mutations that hold it are in the
harness below.

**AND A FALSE POSITIVE IN A CHECK, FIXED IN THE CHECK.** `tests/spawn_sites.rs`
failed on this file: it counts every shipped source that builds a `Command`, and
`PlannedCommand::new(` contains the substring `Command::new(`. `consent.rs` builds
nothing — no `std::process` import anywhere in the file, and its one mention of
`ProcessRequest` is inside a doc comment explaining why `PlannedCommand::new` does
not take one, so `nothing_outside_the_runner_names_a_process_request` passes on it
— and the census was matching a *name* where its rule says *spawn*. The matcher now requires the
character before `Command` to be one that cannot be part of an identifier: true of
every spelling that really builds one, false of every type whose name merely ends
in `Command`. **The rule is unchanged and neither hole a tripwire like this can
have is widened by it** — a bare alias (`use std::process::Command as C;`) was
missed by the old substring search too. A test states the spellings the matcher
must tell apart and states the pair of behaviours around comments, so that a
reader changing one sees the other.

Implement Rust deterministic checks: the four words of the acceptance are four CommandRoles (Format, Check, Lint, Test) with the weights this module argues for, and the second half of the sentence is a design constraint rather than a footnote. cargo fmt rewrites the tree the fingerprint was taken of, so the check is cargo fmt --check: format_command appends that one flag to the discovery's own string, and titled gives the check its own sentence because the role's plain_name describes a rewrite. This is where the module parts company with super::node and super::python, which drop their format role because prettier --write and ruff format are those ecosystems' conventional commands; for Rust the flag is the conventional form. One component, the workspace root, because cargo test with no -p runs the whole workspace and the discovery plans no -p arguments. The toolchain file is evidence about a tool as a configuration file is, and gap_kind separates the two ways a command can be absent: a toolchain SURE could not parse is NotReadable and a tool never mentioned is NotDeclared, with a test holding both that the first is NotReadable and that it does not spread to the two roles cargo itself declares. The binding is the signature: evidence_of takes the fingerprint off CheckResult::project_fingerprint, which is required and has no Default, so None is exactly EvidenceClass::Unknown, which is what a MissingCommand carries.

THE MUTATION THAT COULD NOT BE KILLED, AND A DOC COMMENT THAT WAS FALSE. The first mutation run left one survivor: dropping the second half of RustChecks::is_empty's conjunction. It survived because it is equivalent, not because a test was missing -- for Rust the halves cannot disagree, because CommandRole::Check and CommandRole::Test name cargo and a root Cargo.toml is what declares cargo, so proposed is never empty while missing is not. What the run found is the doc comment above that method, which claimed the second half was the one a mutation can drop and named a project that asked for neither tool as the proof; that project proposes two checks, so both versions answer false. P4-T008.notes: Dependency state: which package ecosystems a project declares packages in, whether the tree SURE walked holds what an install would have put there, and what a check that FAILED over such a project is to be read as. ONE SOURCE FILE ADDED AND ONE LINE OF lib.rs. THE ACCEPTANCE HAS TWO SENTENCES AND THEY PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, which is what shaped the module: 'Missing dependencies are distinguishable from failing project code' asks SURE to say something about installed state, 'Install remains separate approved action' forbids SURE from doing anything about it, and three places in the repository forbid looking at installed state at all -- ECOSYSTEM_DISCOVERY.md:641-645, checks/mod.rs and checks/rust.rs. NOT WHAT IS THIS PROJECT BUT WHAT CAN SURE DO WITH IT RIGHT NOW: discovery refuses to let installed-ness influence what a project IS, and this is a property of the RUN -- it changes between two runs over one unchanged commit and differs between two people on one branch, which is why it does not belong in a discovery result and why it belongs beside the check results it is used to read. THE RULE IS ONE-DIRECTIONAL AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES THE READING SAFE RATHER THAN MERELY INTENDED: a sentinel SURE met means nothing, and a sentinel it did not meet over a walk that finished means one thing. The module never says the packages are installed, not even when it finds the directory an install fills, because what is installed is the package manager's answer -- the directory can be stale, partial, or for a different lockfile than the one in the tree. EVERY WAY OF BEING WRONG IN THE PRESENCE DIRECTION IS SILENT: a false sentinel suppresses a finding and only a true absence can produce one, so the direction of the error is chosen rather than hoped for. THE SEVERITY IS ARGUED FROM THE FROZEN TEXT RATHER THAN CHOSEN: the claim is Severity::Note. MustFix is 'Do not recommend publishing or handing this off' and a fresh clone of a healthy project is in exactly this state, so blocking a hand-off would make SURE refuse to pass judgement on a project it has not been able to check yet. ShouldFixFirst is 'A material reliability or quality risk', which is the wrong SUBJECT as well as the wrong weight -- the risk is to SURE's ability to measure the project's quality and not to the project's quality, and calling an environment fact a quality risk of the code is the precise confusion this task exists to prevent. Two properties follow and neither is bolted on: a Note cannot blocks_hand_off, and can_alone_support_must_fix is about a class rather than a level, so no missing package can become a must_fix about somebody's code. THE TABLE HAS ONE ROW AND THE TWO OMISSIONS ARE ARGUED: Rust is out because there is no gap to find -- cargo test fetches what it needs when it runs, so an absent target is where the next command writes rather than a state to fix first, and checks/rust.rs argues this at length and declines to carry an install step for the same reason. Python is out because absence settles nothing and that is the more interesting omission: a project without an installer gets 'python -m pytest', which the discovery itself calls a command that depends on which interpreter is first on the path (discover/python.rs:1596), and an interpreter first on the path is not in the project, so a walk cannot see it and a project with no .venv may have every one of its packages importable. The honest reason there is no Python row is that SURE cannot tell, not that Python projects do not need installing. THE SENTINEL LIST IS GENEROUS ON PURPOSE AND THE GENEROSITY IS THE SAFETY ARGUMENT: this module's one productive finding is an absence, so a sentinel missing from resolved_into is a project SURE wrongly tells to install packages it already has, while a sentinel that should not have been there costs a SUPPRESSED finding -- the quiet direction. So the list names node_modules AND Yarn's .pnp.cjs and .pnp.js, because a plug'n'play project resolves packages with no node_modules at all and leaving them out would produce a finding on every PnP project in existence; that test is also the half that exercises the walk's ENTRIES rather than its SKIPS, since .pnp.cjs is an ordinary file while node_modules reaches the reading as a Skipped. A push review named crates/sure-core/src/runtime_start.rs and carried NO finding text, so the claim was verified by reading the file's security surface rather than by trusting the notification, and the reading turned up a real defect: last_words places a service's own bytes inside a sentence SURE prints, a service is a project's process, text_lossy replaces only what is not valid UTF-8, so every control character except the newline the lines were split on can reach the quote -- and a lone carriage return or an escape sequence such as an escape plus [2K can erase the line SURE's own report of the failure is printed on. A FAILING SERVICE COULD THEREFORE ERASE THE REPORT OF ITS OWN FAILURE WHILE A PERSON WAS READING IT: a false green in the terminal rather than in the verdict, which is the class of defect this product treats as the most serious one. The workspace already had the treatment -- setup.rs's in_a_sentence escapes project text for exactly this reason and in nearly these words, and diagnostics::Field does the same for a value in a message, both built on redact::escape_control_characters -- and what is new here is the KIND of text: every other caller escapes a name a project chose, and this is the first place where it is whatever a project's process decided to write. The fix is one call placed BEFORE the character bound so the bound's own doc stays true of what a reader sees, and the test asserts the invariant -- !quoted.chars().any(char::is_control) -- rather than the two characters that prompted it. The catch was verified by hand: the call removed, the test run, FAILED at exit 101, and the file restored to its committed blob

P5-T002.notes: Runtime service smoke: starting a project's own service, asking it one question, and stopping it. ONE SOURCE FILE ADDED, ONE TEST FILE ADDED, ONE LINE OF lib.rs, ONE CENSUS RULE AND ONE PARAGRAPH OF support.rs. The task's sentence is 'Supported service can be started/probed/terminated' and 'Startup failure remains explicit', and the module is arranged so that the second is structural rather than documented: THE TABLE OF ENDINGS IS TOTAL, every arm of it has a status, and the two arms that could be mistaken for a pass are the two the tests are written against. The chain is ProbePlan::of -> PermissionPlan::add -> Enforcement::of -> Supervisor::start -> StartSmoke::run, and StartSmoke::of takes an Enforcement RATHER THAN A COMMAND, which is enforce.rs's own rule applied one level up: the module looks the admitted command up by the probe's OWN check id, so a smoke check cannot run a command a mode stopped and cannot run one that was planned for a different check. Two tests hold the halves of that, and the second is the interesting one -- the enforcement admits two commands and the DECOY IS ADMITTED FIRST, so a lookup that took the first command it found would take the wrong one, and the decoy's child writes a marker on its way out that the test asserts is not there. Without the decoy that test would be about the plan rather than about the lookup. THE ROW WITH TWO WAYS IN IS THE ONE A START CHECK EXISTS FOR: 'it ended by itself' is a failure whether it ended inside the window or after it, in two sentences that differ in which fact they lead with, because A SERVICE THAT EXITS IS NOT A SERVICE WHATEVER IT PRINTED ON THE WAY OUT and start is the one script whose whole meaning is that this keeps running. A start that came up, answered SURE's question and then ended by itself is therefore a failure too, which is the case a check that only asked about the port would have called green. The other three rows are the pass -- THE PROBE'S OWN STATUS, CARRIED RATHER THAN RE-DECIDED, which is what keeps this module from becoming a second opinion about what a port said -- the warning for a service that came up with nothing to ask, and two error rows for a program that never started and a run SURE cannot vouch for. A QUESTION IS ONLY ASKED WHILE THE PROCESS SURE STARTED IS STILL RUNNING, and that is a rule rather than an ordering: a port that answers after SURE's own process is gone may be answering for something SURE did not start, and a pass built on that would be a claim about a service SURE never saw come up. THE HARDEST ROW NEEDED A SECOND PROCESS RATHER THAN A LONGER SLEEP, because the first instrument was flaky rather than slow -- when the death and the end of the exchange are the same instant the runner can poll in the gap and report Cancelled, which is the wrong row. A case-insensitive repo grep for `one[- _]time|allow once|allow_once|allowonce` returned exactly three things — the `PROTECTION_MODE.md:29` mock-up `[Allow once] [Do not allow]`, this task's own acceptance string, and an unrelated line in `probe.rs` about "a caller's one-time cost". So the acceptance was not "add three detectors"; it was "make what is already detected reach a user, and give it the override the document already promises".

 Criterion: the three dangers, driven. The supervisor's own probe (target/tmp/sup-p13t005-probe2.ps1, output sup-p13t005-probe2.txt), through `target\debug\sure.exe` with payloads the supervisor wrote, into a scratch store under `%TEMP%` and a scratch project outside the repository. A project whose `sure.yaml` says `execution: mode: host_confirmed`. **Broad delete**: `rm -rf build/` with no grant → block, exit 1, "This names a whole location rather than one file, so it could change many files at once. That may be a valid refactor, and it can also remove working code. A harness hook cannot ask you about this, so SURE does not allow it." Then `hook allow-once --tool Shell --command "rm -rf build/"` → exit 0; the same request → **allow, exit 0**, "…You recorded a one-time allowance for this exact request, and this use spends it, so SURE would let this one through. No further request with these words would be allowed."; the same request a third time → **block, exit 1** with the danger sentence. **Force push**: `git push --force origin main` → block/1, "This would replace commits that were already published. Anything built on them — someone else's branch, a release, a review — is left pointing at work that is no longer there…"; with its own grant → allow/0 with the allowance sentence. **Sensitive read**: a project also saying `protection: mode: strict`, `Read` of `.env` → block/1 with P13-T004's credentials sentence; `hook allow-once --tool Read --path .env` → exit 0; re-read → **allow/0**; re-read again → **block/1**. So each of the three is represented, each has a working override path, and each is spent exactly once.

 The direction that keeps it honest, driven: a grant belongs to one request and leaks to no other. Fresh store, a grant for `rm -rf build/`, then a held `git push --force origin main` with no grant of its own → block/1, and then the delete the grant *was* for → still allow/0. So the force push neither consumed nor was covered by the delete's allowance. A line SURE refuses to read is held and offers nothing: `rm -rf "my dir"` and `cargo test && rm -rf .` both → block/1 with the plain consent sentence, **no danger named**, and therefore no allowance that could ever cover them — which is the fail-closed direction, because `read_simple_command` answering `None` is exactly the state SURE was in before the function existed. The writer refuses a window it will not record: `--minutes 20000` and `--minutes 0` both → exit 5, "SURE will not record an allowance lasting that long." with the detail naming the 1..1440 bound and why.

 No second rule engine, checked rather than asserted. `allowance.rs` (the new module, 485 lines) contains no command name — a grep for `"rm"`, `"git"`, `"del"`, `"curl"`, `"chmod"`, `"sudo"`, `"bash"`, `"sh"` in it returns nothing — and never calls `classify`; its imports are `serde`, `sure_domain::ids::FingerprintId` and the store's own types. Every dangerous label comes from one path: `assessed_request` reads a danger only for `NeedsConsent` (`hook_protection.rs:426-429`) and only through `claimed_danger` → `command_danger` (`:605-684`), which calls `safety::read_simple_command` and then `safety::classify` and takes a danger **only** when `classification.source()` is `Source::Rule` — so a program the table does not know, or text it cannot read, names nothing rather than being reported as SURE's own failure to classify.

 The shell-reading decision, named and inspected because it is where a false green would hide. A harness sends one string; `safety::classify` takes a program with its argv and has no string variant, "because splitting shell text is itself the act of starting a shell" (`safety.rs:240-247`). The worker's answer is `read_simple_command`, which **refuses first and reads only what is left**: any of `" ' \ $ ` ; & | < > ( ) { } ! # % ^` or CR/LF/NUL makes the whole line unreadable and the answer `None`. The direction is what matters and it is the safe one: `None` removes nothing, because a shell request is held whatever the reading says — the only thing the reading changes is whether a user *can* spend an allowance on it. `~ * ? [ ]` are deliberately kept, and the reasons are sound in the same direction: `rm -rf *` is read as `["rm","-rf","*"]`, `rm` is unconditionally destructive in the table, and `*` makes the whole-location test fire — so keeping them makes SURE hold *more*, not less. The stated cost is real and documented: a Windows-style path inside a shell line contains `\`, so the line is not read, not named, and not offerable for an allowance.

 The atomicity claim, verified at the mechanism rather than at the prose. `spend_allowance` reads the outstanding rows, decides, and writes the use inside `self.transaction(...)` (`store/mod.rs:581-610`), and `transaction` is `execute_batch("BEGIN IMMEDIATE")` at `:908` with the doc at `:899` explaining that it takes the write lock now rather than at the first write. A deferred transaction would have let two processes both read "outstanding" and serialise only at write time, which is the double-spend the method exists to prevent; with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` the second process blocks before it reads. The `insert`/`write_row` split the worker made is behaviour-preserving, checked: `insert` still validates, takes the timestamp and opens the transaction (`:841-861`), and `write_row` (`:870`) is the INSERT with no transaction of its own — which is what lets `spend_allowance` open one transaction and still use it.

The reason for a fourth kind rather than reusing `Approval` is stated in the code and holds up: `approvals()` filters on `RecordKind::Approval` exactly (`store/mod.rs:190-196`) and `is_approval()` is `matches!(self, Self::Approval)` (`record.rs:189-191`), so a second document shape under that name would have made the approval audit trail stop reading rather than skip what it does not understand.

 A defect found while verifying, which is not this task's and now has an owner. **`sure hook allow-once` reports success for an allowance that provably can never be spent.** Driven: a project whose `sure.yaml` says `execution: mode: inspect_only` — the default — records a grant, exits 0, and prints "SURE recorded a one-time allowance for tool 'Shell', for the request 'rm -rf build/'." followed by "SURE would then let that one request through, if SURE names it as deleting a whole location, overwriting published commits, or reading a file of credentials." The request it was recorded for is then still blocked, unchanged, with "The current execution mode does not permit this action.", however many times it is sent. The cause is not a defective spend path: under a mode that does not run project code, `consent::decide_for` answers an arbitrary command `Denied` rather than `NeedsConsent` (`consent.rs:491-501`, because `CommandClass::Destructive.required_permission()` is `None` at `sure-domain/src/execution.rs:631`), and `assess_request` reads a danger only for `NeedsConsent`, so no danger is ever named and `with_any_allowance` returns at its first line (`hook.rs:416-418`). That refusal is deliberate, correct and documented — "an allowance is not a way to run under settings the user did not change". What is wrong is only what the person is told at the moment they record the grant: the command has `--project`, could read the mode, and instead reports a success and a promise that this project's settings make unreachable. The safe direction holds throughout — nothing dangerous is allowed — so this is a false reassurance and a silent no-op, not a false green, and it is **P13-T010**, added 2026-09-19 after P13-T009 and deliberately placed there so the ready order is unchanged. The related silence the document already accepts — that the *subject* is not checked at write time, because there is no request to read then — is deliberately left alone; the mode, unlike the subject, is knowable at write time.

 The honest limits, recorded rather than smoothed over. **The override is reachable only where the project's own config requests running project code.** Under the default `inspect_only` a destructive shell request is `Denied`, so no danger is named and no allowance can be spent; `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md` states this ("a mode that does not permit it… an allowance is not a way to run under settings the user did not change") and the code comment at `hook_protection.rs:423-425` gives the reason. The consequence is that the acceptance is met for projects that request `host_confirmed`, and the command that `host_confirmed` is read from is the project's own file with no user arbitration — the gap `hook.rs:510-512` already attributes to **P13-T009**. Nothing here is a claim that a harness honours the answer: both integrations stay capability tier 1 (Observed), every sentence is in the "SURE would / SURE does not" voice, and the allowance sentence says the use is spent without ever saying something ran. The named coverage gaps are left named: `git clean -fdx` and `git reset --hard` are destructive without naming anything SURE can bound and are therefore not overridable; a shell read of a secret is covered by the blanket shell block but not named as a sensitive read; widening any of those means widening `safety`'s rules, which belongs to whoever owns the classifier.

THE ACCEPTANCE IS "warn/block/allow-once decision recorded locally without secrets", and the four hard points the brief named are each answered in the source rather than in the report. "Without secrets" is answered by STORING LESS: DecisionRecord carries no subject, no command line and no path, because nothing matches against a decision -- a grant keeps its subject exactly as typed because a grant is matched against a request, and a decision is read by a person afterwards and the request's own words are already in the event payload the row hangs from, redacted once. Proved by a test that reads back every file the store directory holds: the token ghp_0123456789abcdefghij appears in no byte of any of them, AND the redacted form https://***@github.com/acme/app.git does appear -- the second half is what makes the first an absence rather than an empty loop, and the test says so in its own comment. "Where the row hangs" is event_id, which is the join both decisions_for_session and delete_sessions use, so a decision inherits the event's retention and the user's delete; SessionEventStore::persist_decision refuses INSIDE the transaction when the event is not in the store, because a row nothing can show or delete would sit outside docs/security/PRIVACY.md's promise. "Allow-once vs ordinary allow" is the two fields beside the kind -- danger is Some only where SURE named the request dangerous, allowance names the grant row that was spent -- both carried from the decision already taken, with nothing re-read or re-decided. "What a failed write does" is nothing to the answer: the kind and the exit code are unchanged and a sentence is added to the reason, so the one outcome the code cannot produce is a missing record that nothing mentions.

Accepted 2026-09-19 on the hand-back commit 9eda950, verified independently: the six gates run by the supervisor from native PowerShell, the new test file and the new document read rather than counted, the one defect this acceptance sent back reproduced here before the fix and re-measured after it, the table's own census re-derived from the page rather than read out of either the page's prose or the hand-back's message, and the Unix launchers executed under Git Bash as the weaker evidence that is labelled as such.

THE ACCEPTANCE IS "fail-open/fail-closed behaviour is explicit for each harness/event and surfaced in docs", AND THE HALF THAT WAS MISSING WAS THE HALF NOTHING MEASURED. `crates/sure-testkit/tests/integration_thinness.rs` asserted what a launcher's *text* contains — that the script resolves the binary, names its source, relays a status — and every one of those assertions passes on a launcher that then drops the status it relayed. The four failing inputs (`sure hook ingest` with empty stdin, with non-JSON, with an unknown `--source`, with an event type no manifest maps) existed only as in-process assertions about a `Report` value, which is a statement about a function and not about the process a harness talks to. A launcher that found `sure`, ran it, and exited 0 whatever SURE answered satisfied every check in this tree before this commit, and that is the false green the task exists to remove. One correction to my own brief rides with it: the brief said no test ever executes a launcher script, and that is false — `integration_thinness.rs` spawns `sure-mcp.ps1` in the four `#[cfg(windows)]` tests at `:513`, `:562`, `:609` and `:663`, which I re-verified by mapping every mention of the script in that file to its enclosing function. The worker reported the error instead of repeating it, and the brief's three cited line numbers were off by one as well.

WHAT THE TREE NOW HOLDS, AND WHAT EACH PIECE CANNOT OBSERVE. `crates/sure-testkit/tests/hook_failure_semantics.rs` (875 lines, 5 tests) spawns each *packaged* launcher — four `.ps1` on Windows, three `.sh` through `/bin/sh` on Unix, selected per platform from the tree rather than from a hand-written list, so a launcher added without a row is a failure and not an omission — against a stand-in that answers 0, 1 or 5 and writes a distinct marker to each stream, then asserts the launcher's own exit status and both streams; and then the same launchers with SURE nowhere to be found, where each must exit 0 and write nothing to stdout. `crates/sure-cli/tests/cli_contract.rs` (+224: two tests and an `ingest_argv` helper) drives the real binary through the four failing inputs and asserts exit 5, no `decision` key, no store file created, and history reporting nothing. `docs/integrations/HOOK_FAILURE_SEMANTICS.md` (286 lines) is the row-per-harness-per-event page `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md:105` requires and `docs/architecture/CONFIG_AUTHORITY.md:152` names this task as owning, and a fifth test reads it, derives the harnesses and events from `integrations/*/hooks/hooks.json` and from the launchers present in the tree, and fails on a wired event with no row, on a semantics cell that is not one of the three permitted values, on a `cannot confirm` that names no remedy, and on an evidence cell naming a test that does not exist in the workspace. Re-derived here rather than read: 20 rows, one per wired event across four harnesses, and the cells are **13 `fail-open`, 1 `fail-closed`, 6 `cannot confirm`.**

WHAT IT CANNOT OBSERVE IS THE HALF THE PAGE REFUSES TO INVENT, AND THAT IS WHY THE UNCERTAINTY IS A RESULT RATHER THAN A GAP. Nothing in this repository observes a harness. The tests observe SURE's exit status and streams; the page's harness-side column is quoted from a named vendor page read on 2026-09-19, or says `cannot confirm` and names what would settle it. The six cells are not one kind of uncertainty and the page says so: cursor `preToolUse`, where the vendor page's general fail-open rule for a non-2 non-zero exit and its permission-hook rule for a response that does not match the hook's schema point opposite ways on the shape this launcher actually sends; three Codex events the page read here does not define; two Copilot event names it does not define either. The record keeps the two halves apart in the same table, which is the only way a reader can tell a measured answer from a quoted one.

TWO FINDINGS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED, BECAUSE SETTLING EITHER IS NOT THIS TASK'S TO DO. Copilot: `grep -rn copilot crates/` returns nothing, so `--source copilot` exits 5 for every event, while `integrations/copilot/README.md:156` says the adapter must fail open, and the Copilot hooks reference makes `preToolUse` fail-closed on a non-zero exit — the two statements disagree in the direction that denies every tool call. No normaliser was added and the README was not softened; the page states what was measured and recommends treating the package as what its own manifest calls it, a placeholder. Claude Code: its hooks page makes exit 2 the only blocking status, so a SURE block (exit 1) and a SURE failure (exit 5) are both non-blocking there — recorded from upstream in the same page and marked as recorded rather than measured. Two further gaps are named as open rather than left for a reader to find: every launcher script is packaged `100644`, so a fresh Unix checkout cannot start one by path even though the Codex manifest names it directly, and nothing in this repository records what a harness does on a hook timeout, with the four vendor pages disagreeing about how much it matters.

THE DEFECT THIS ACCEPTANCE SENT BACK WOULD HAVE TURNED CI RED ON TWO OF THREE PLATFORMS, AND IT WAS IN THE TEST'S SETUP RATHER THAN IN ITS ASSERTION. The missing-binary test emptied `PATH` to make `sure` unfindable, and on Unix that also hides `cat`, which `integrations/cursor/scripts/sure-hook.sh:13` uses to drain stdin — so `/bin/sh` writes `cat: command not found` to stderr and the test, whose helper asserts stderr is empty for that case, fails on macOS and Ubuntu while passing on Windows. I reproduced it before sending it back — `cat=/usr/bin/cat`, `sure=not found`, and the cursor launcher's stderr carrying the shell's own diagnostic — and I refused the two cheap fixes: weakening the assertion, and putting `2>/dev/null` on the drain, which would silence a real diagnostic to satisfy a test. The fix keeps the assertion byte for byte and changes the environment instead: on Unix `PATH` becomes `/usr/bin:/bin` and a new `assert_sure_cannot_be_found` walks those entries and the two absolute fallbacks the launchers try (`/opt/homebrew/bin/sure`, `/usr/local/bin/sure`) and fails loudly, naming the path, if this machine has one — so the test refuses to run where it would prove nothing rather than passing where it proves nothing. `SURE_BIN` stays removed and `HOME`/`LOCALAPPDATA` still point at an empty directory, which is what covers the Cargo and per-user install locations; Windows still empties `PATH`, which its `.ps1` launchers tolerate because they call nothing outside the shell. The fix is 2 files, +79/−5, and no changed line in it mentions `silent`, `stderr.is_empty`, `stderr_has` or `stderr_lacks` — the assertion the send-back was about is untouched.

That numeral is also in the delivered page, at `HOOK_FAILURE_SEMANTICS.md:176`, and it is the one prose defect this acceptance corrected rather than merely recorded: `Five rows say cannot confirm` becomes `Six rows say cannot confirm`, one word, no behaviour touched, the page's own test still green. Nothing about a verdict moves either way, and the reason both are worth the space is that both are counts stated without being re-derived, which is the class this repository's evidence discipline exists for.

THE VERIFICATION IS THE SUPERVISOR'S OWN RUNS AND NOT THE HAND-BACK'S. Six gates from native PowerShell on `9eda950`: `fmt` 0, `clippy` 0, the workspace suite 0 with **64 cargo headers (59 `Running` + 5 `Doc-tests`) against 74 `test result:` lines, 2515 passed by the parent rule, 2525 as the raw sum, 0 failed, 12 ignored** — the two instruments agreeing, which item 103's script refuses to proceed without — `validate-bootstrap` 0, `taskctl validate` 0, and the sixth gate 0 over both Unix targets with its usual `NOT CHECKED` section naming `sure-core` and `sure-cli`. ONE CLAIM IN THE HAND-BACK WAS NOT REPRODUCED AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN DROPPED. The worker reported a `cargo test --workspace` run that exited 101 with no failing test in the output, and disclosed it. I ran the workspace suite three more times and the focused launcher suite five more times on this tree: no recurrence, exit 0 every time. That is "not reproduced", not "flake-free"; the cause is unidentified and it is written down because a 101 nobody can reproduce is a fact about this tree until something explains it.
