## The departure the hand-back flagged, adjudicated

The brief's §4.1 says a project may be *more restrictive* than the user, and the
worker deliberately did not apply that to `execution.mode`: it made the mode the
user's own and refused a project's move in either direction, and flagged the
departure rather than burying it. I checked the shape of the settings rather than
the sentence, and the worker's argument is right and understated.

`resolve()` returns the default unless `rank(value) > rank(default)`
(`authority.rs:673`). For this setting the default **is** the strictest value
there is — `ExecutionConfig::default()` is `inspect_only`
(`config/mod.rs:145`), and `Config::default()` supplies it for a project with no
file at all as well as for one that says nothing. A "stricter of the two" rule
would therefore return `inspect_only` **unconditionally**, so a user's grant
could never take effect at all — not merely when a `sure.yaml` happens to be
present, which is how the hand-back put it. The rule as implemented is the only
one available without inventing a "was this field named" signal that this
configuration deliberately does not have, and `CONFIG_AUTHORITY.md` now states
the rule, the reason, and what a project's ask leaves on the record. Accepted.

The contrast is in the same commit and it is what makes the exception a rule
rather than a preference: for the recording *retention* the same layer still
prefers the stricter of the two, because there the default is not the strictest
value — `a_project_file_cannot_outlast_the_users_retention` (hook.rs) writes a
user file naming three days and a project naming thirty, and asserts the row is
kept for three, with a comment saying a build that silently kept three while
reporting thirty would pass a test that only read
`Authority::full_recording_retention_days`. So the four settings are resolved by
one rule that reads the shape of each — the mode and the consent fall to the
user alone because their strictest value is also their default, the retention and
the protection mode arbitrate because theirs is not.

Accepted on the second submission, after ONE send-back, over four worker commits.

The task's two criteria are "Missing intent never yields full requirement fulfillment" and "Explicit intent mismatch can yield grounded finding", and neither is about defective code. P14-T004's trap was three routes that all answered the same word, so a checker answering cannot_confirm to everything would have satisfied every positive assertion that task could write. This task's trap is the same shape with two different stuck reporters: a reporter that always answered "I cannot confirm this matches your request" satisfies criterion 1, and one that always answered "requirement not met" satisfies criterion 2. The brief named both before dispatch, and the defence is structural -- criterion 1 is swept across the whole evidence-count space rather than spot-checked, and each fixture carries a control that is the fixture with exactly one thing moved and that must reach the opposite answer. A fixture with no control was a send-back named in advance.

WHAT WAS ACCEPTED. fixtures/adversarial/missing-user-intent/ fills the manifest case that had a row and no directory since the manifest was written -- it is no longer among the four ids with no fixture directory. fixtures/adversarial/intent-mismatch/ has no manifest case and is named in FIXTURES_WITHOUT_A_MANIFEST_CASE with the nearest row and why renaming it after that row would make the row grade something it was not written for. CRITERION 2 IS READ AS A PERMISSION, AND THAT WAS DECIDED BEFORE DISPATCH. compare_intent_to_project has exactly one production caller, pipeline.rs:1262, which consumes only .findings. An unmatched requirement yields one CheckProposal from declared_intent_proposal, which hard-wires Note, Inference and critical == false through gravity_of with GapKind::DeclaredIntent, and finding_gravity's (GapKind::DeclaredIntent, _) => INFORMATIONAL holds on every reach. false_completion_aggregator then files it as style noise, never material. So it is not a Finding at all, Finding::is_grounded is never reached on it, and supports_severity admits Inference only at a non-blocking severity. The strict reading -- is_grounded() == true of a Finding -- is false today, and making it true would mean promoting a keyword-search miss to a hand-off blocker: it contradicts the manifest's note and not-release-blocking row, contradicts the gravity rule and its own unit test, and turns every requirement SURE fails to keyword-match into a false must-fix. The fixture therefore pins the measured level by equality AND pins the ceiling as a ceiling, asserting AssessmentSource::Inference.supports_severity(Severity::MustFix) as a fact of the source rather than reading it off the proposal. The decision was written into the brief and the worker was required to overturn it only by measurement, first line of the hand-back. The hand-back confirmed it and nothing contradicted it.

WHY THE NO-DANGER RUNS ARE IN THE FIXTURES RATHER THAN LEFT OUT. The trap this task was dispatched around is that "the dangerous action is blocked" is satisfied by a build with Danger deleted entirely, because base_decision (hook_protection.rs:1468) blocks NeedsConsent with a sentence naming no danger. So each fixture carries both halves: runs that must be held AND name their danger, and runs that must be held with no danger named -- an unforced push, a stacked line, a read of a key file in a directory the classifier cannot see whole -- so that a product which names a danger everywhere reddens exactly as loudly as one that names none. Accepted 2026-09-19 on the third hand-back, `a1fe4f6` ("P13-T010: read a tool name in the vocabulary that claims it, and refuse a grant no setting can make spendable"), verified independently: the six gates from native PowerShell, every probe in the brief re-driven by the supervisor, and the two cases that need the user's own settings file driven in-process and read back from the store. It was sent back twice before this, and both send-backs were measurements rather than preferences — the task took three workers because the first two hand-backs each shipped a false sentence, and one of the two sentences was the supervisor's error first.

WHAT THE TASK IS FOR. `sure hook allow-once` writes a one-time allowance for a request SURE would otherwise hold, and under the settings a user starts in the request it names is not held at all: `ExecutionConfig::default()` is `inspect_only`, a destructive command under a mode that runs no project code is answered `Denied` rather than `NeedsConsent`, and `assess_request` reads a danger only for `NeedsConsent` — so the writer reported a success and a promise ("SURE would then let that one request through") that this project's own settings make unreachable, and nothing in the build writes the user's own `sure.yaml`, so it was the sentence every user of this build read. The acceptance is that the command either refuses and says why or records and says what will actually happen, that the reason names the setting in the user's terms, that a confirmation which *can* be spent reads differently from one that cannot, and that the store matches whichever was chosen.

THE FIRST SEND-BACK: THE REFUSAL WAS KEYED ON THE WRONG SET. The writer asked `acts_a_request_could_be_held_for(mode, permissions, protection)` — the union over all five danger witnesses, for every tool — and recorded whenever that union was non-empty. The question is whether the settings make *every matching request* unanswerable. Measured on `e268777` in a scratch project whose `sure.yaml` is `protection: {mode: strict}` with `execution: {mode: inspect_only}`, a configuration a user reaches by taking only the second half of the advice the refusal itself gives: `allow-once --tool Shell --command "rm -rf build/"` exits 0 and records the row; the exact matching Cursor `preToolUse` event then exits 1 with "The current execution mode does not permit this action.", and the decision row reads back `allowance: null`. The allowance is never consulted, because `decide` refuses before any danger is read. Both line 0 and line 3 were falsified by that read-back, and the fix landed as `2ec2f38` + `e270fe8` rather than by rewriting the measurement. The file's own test `a_grant_carries_the_acts_the_settings_in_force_leave_for_it` had asserted the wrong behaviour, which is why the brief named it instead of leaving the worker to find it.

THE SECOND SEND-BACK: THE ACTS WERE RIGHT AND THE SENTENCES WERE WRONG FOR THREE NAMES, one of them offering a remedy that was measured not to work. Defect A — under **default** settings `--tool Write` and `--tool Delete` exit 5 with no store directory and a sentence whose only clause about a setting names `protection.mode: standard`, which is provably not the cause: set it to `strict` and the same command refuses again with "already `strict` … nothing firmer to set". So the refusal named a setting that was not standing in the way and offered no remedy at all, and the opening's own escape hatch — "for as long as these settings are in force" — was false for those two names. Defect B — `Edit` is in `CLAUDE_CODE_TOOLS` as `WriteProjectFile` and not in `CURSOR_TOOLS`, so the union the first brief demanded answers `{WriteProjectFile, ArbitraryCommand}` and takes the more permissive reading: under default settings `--tool Edit` was refused with the `host_confirmed` remedy, and taking that advice (so `run_project_code` is granted) made `allow-once --tool Edit --path src/lib.rs` **record** `acts=[BroadDelete, ForcePush]`, which then **neither** a Claude Code `Edit` nor a Cursor `Edit` could spend. THE ACCEPTANCE IS "make the non-Windows configuration checkable from Windows", AND IT IS NARROWER THAN THE TITLE SOUNDS, which is the first thing the record has to say. The machine this project is developed on is Windows, `cargo clippy` with no `--target` compiles the Windows `cfg` set, and in that set every `#[cfg(not(windows))]` item is not compiled at all — so a break inside the non-Windows arms is invisible here and can only appear on a runner. That is not hypothetical: it is the class the 75-run red streak belonged to, because on Linux and macOS the job died at clippy and the Unix tests behind it were unrun rather than failing. What the deliverable does is compile the Unix arms here: one file, `scripts/check-non-windows.mjs`, which for each of `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` and `x86_64-apple-darwin` runs the same command as the local clippy gate with `--target <triple>`, `--all-targets` included. `--all-targets` is load-bearing and not decoration: the defect that caused the streak was three helper functions used only from Windows-gated tests, and integration tests are a target a plain `cargo clippy` does not reach.

WHAT IT REACHES IS 12 OF 116 PLATFORM-CONDITIONAL SITES, AND THE NUMBER IS IN THE FILE RATHER THAN IN THIS NOTE ONLY. The census — `cfg(windows)`, `cfg(not(windows))`, `cfg(unix)`, `target_os`, `target_family` over `crates/**/*.rs` — is 116: sure-domain 0, sure-protocol 0, sure-testkit 12, sure-core 100, sure-cli 4, with 22 `target_os`-qualified sites, every one of them in sure-core, which I re-measured rather than took from the hand-back. `sure-core` and `sure-cli` cannot be compiled for either Unix target on this machine, so 104 sites are outside the check, all the `target_os` arms among them. The blocker is C and there is more of it than the brief said: `sure-core` takes `rusqlite` with `bundled`, so `libsqlite3-sys` compiles `sqlite3.c` for the target, AND it takes `ureq`, which reaches `ring 0.17.14` through `rustls` and compiles its own C — both traced in `Cargo.lock`, and both in a build script, which is why `cargo check --target` fails exactly where clippy does, why `--no-deps` does not avoid it, and why the two commands that look like escapes are not: `CC_FORCE_DISABLE=1` errors rather than skipping, and `LIBSQLITE3_SYS_USE_PKG_CONFIG=1` gets past SQLite and dies on `ring`. The worker corrected the brief's "one C library" and the correction is right.

THE MEASURE THAT MATTERS IS NOT THE EXIT CODE, IT IS WHICH DEFECTS THE CHECK WOULD HAVE CAUGHT, AND THE ANSWER IS ONE OF THREE. Of the three defects the streak's census recorded: the three Unix-dead helpers in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/integration_thinness.rs` — caught, and that is the defect that made the streak; the Windows-path assertions in `sure-core`'s `candidate_context.rs` and `recording_projection.rs` — not caught, because they live in the crate the check cannot compile and because they are assertions that fail when Unix code RUNS; `recheck_lifecycle.rs`'s Unix branch asserting the wrong `kept_open` — not caught, for both of those reasons. So the check covers the FORM the streak took and none of the assertion defects, and the file says so in its own header rather than leaving a reader to work it out. The demonstration is the supervisor's own run and not the hand-back's: deleting the three `#[cfg(windows)]` attributes at `integration_thinness.rs:448,464,486` makes it exit 1 naming `powershell`, `launcher_scratch` and `stub_binary` at the shifted lines 448, 463 and 484, ending `error: could not compile "sure-testkit" (test "integration_thinness") due to 3 previous errors`; restoring the file byte-identically (sha256 `b70eb1b0…`, `git status --porcelain` empty, followed by a touch because `Copy-Item` preserves `LastWriteTime`) makes it exit 0. The missing-target path was exercised on a copy with `x86_64-unknown-freebsd` in place of darwin: exit 1, "Nothing was checked", and the `rustup target add` line printed.

IT REFUSES RATHER THAN PASSES QUIETLY, AND THE ONE PLACE IT EXITS 0 IS STATED. `rustup` missing, or a target not installed, is exit 1 with the command that closes it. A whole-workspace failure that is not the missing C compiler is exit 1 with the compiler's output printed whole. When the failure IS the C compiler it asks again with `--exclude sure-core --exclude sure-cli`, prints what passed, and then a `--- NOT CHECKED ---` section naming the two crates, the two C libraries, and the `CC_x86_64_unknown_linux_gnu` / `CC_x86_64_apple_darwin` variables that would close the gap — naming `zig cc` as a compiler that installs without administrator rights and recording that this repository has not installed or verified it. That path exits 0, and the choice is argued in the file rather than left to be inferred: exit 0 means every crate this could check is clean for both Unix targets, the section naming what was not checked prints unconditionally on that path, and the last line says the run "says nothing about their Unix configuration". Exit 1 there would leave the gate permanently red on a machine with no cross C compiler while detecting nothing the section does not already report, and a check nobody can afford to run is a check nobody runs. The whole-workspace attempt is made FIRST, so nothing in the file is a standing claim that those crates cannot be checked: the day a cross C compiler is present the excluded command is never composed and that section never prints.

Accepted 2026-09-19 on the corrected hand-back, `9ee733d` ("P13-T011: correct what the layer rule says about `allow_project_write`"), verified independently: the six gates from native PowerShell, four of the probes re-driven by the supervisor at the process boundary with fixtures of its own, the three allowance sentences driven and their stores read back, and the layer rule measured with one instrument three times. WHAT THE TASK IS FOR. Nothing in this build granted `Permission::WriteProject`, and `required_permission` sends `WriteProjectFile` and `DeleteProjectFile` to it, `decide` denies on a missing permission **before** it consults the mode, `ProjectRequest`'s seven variants included no arm that returns it, `Authority::permissions()` starts from `inspect_only()`, and the two literal `write_project` assignments in the tree are both inside `#[cfg(test)]`. So every file change was refused in every execution mode under every configuration — an ordinary edit, in the most permissive configuration this build has, answered Block — while `docs/security/PROTECTION_MODE.md:38-42` said `strict` "differs from `standard` on the categories named above and on nothing else" and then listed where a change is held, which read plainly is a promise that an ordinary change is not held under `standard`. The tree was consistent with two products and the brief said so in its first paragraph: either refusing every change is the posture — SURE is a checking layer and not a coding-agent orchestrator — or a change must be grantable from the user's own settings file and never from a project's `sure.yaml`, the way `P13-T009` and `P15-T022` settled `execution.mode` and `privacy.full_recording`. Either answer was acceptable; a hand-back that changed code without first saying which one it found and what measurement decided it would be sent back.

THE DECISION, AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDED IT. The second reading, decided by a controlled pair at the process boundary — the same payload twice with one thing moved. With `execution.mode: host_confirmed` in the **user's own** settings file, a Claude Code `PreToolUse` event naming `Edit` for `src/lib.rs` was answered Block, "The current execution mode does not permit this action." The mode was not the cause and could not be made to be: `ActionKind::WriteProjectFile` does not execute project code, so `executes_project_code()` (`crates/sure-domain/src/execution.rs:80`) is false of it, and with the permission granted `decide` reaches `Allowed` in **every** mode.
